newsitem.title: UK: Chartists add voices to strong dollar chorus.
newsitem.headline: Chartists add voices to strong dollar chorus.

text.p: Chart watchers are adding their voices to the chorus of dollar bulls and point to near-term technical objectives of 1.72 and, further out, up to 1.76 marks.

Tuesday's break above last week's 33-month high at 1.6755 marks underlined the prevailing bullish dollar mood, but the penetration of a 6-1/2 year trendline around 1.6830 on Wednesday has prompted a rethink of dollar life above 1.70, the next major upside objective.

A hold above the 1.6820/30 trendline, drawn from the dollar's peaks in July 1991 and February 1994, effectively takes out the last significant trend resistance point since blocking a further dollar upmove, analysts said.
"Although it's not a major trendline, it does mark the top of the dollar's downtrend from early 1990," said a U.S. bank analyst.
Analysts warned, however, the 1.68 and 1.69 levels would be key levels the dollar has to hold to maintain the upward momentum.
"The 1.68 level is a big threshold," said Brian Kiely, treasury technician at Royal Bank of Scotland. "We are targeting 1.72 marks but it has to hold two full days above 1.68 before we target that."
The dollar did test higher in Europe earlier, touching briefly 1.6935 marks before retreating back to the mid-1.68 marks area.
Apart from relatively minor psychological resistance at the 1.69 level, the dollar still has to overcome resistance around 1.6950 marks.

"There is a retracement level in the 1.6950/70 area which is the 50 percent retracement from about around 2.05 marks to around 1.35," said Karen Jones, technical analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston in London.
This is the dollar decline from its 1989 high to the low in March 1995.
Clearance of this resistance point then sets up the psychological 1.70 mark level and leaves little in its way to territory above 1.72 marks.
CSFB's Jones targets 1.7250 on the upside, which represents an historic resistance level stretching back to 1988.
Above here, significant targets lie at the August 1994 peak of 1.7485 and then in early 1995 when the dollar traded just shy of 1.77 marks.

However, Royal Bank of Scotland's Kiely warns of a near-term correction before a move higher but only sees it pulling back to the 1.6750 level, the dollar's top from last week, and then down to around the 1.6650 area.
"On a break below here, 1.6586/63 becomes the focus," said Kiely.
